Background concepts / WEBFRONT

Modern C++ and asynchrony

Callback ownership, task suspension and local cancellation.

Notation conventions

Function names, types, commands, options and filenames appear in monospace, for example describe, wf test or main.cpp. Italics introduce a term at its definition. Code blocks give the fragments to enter; the preceding text states their location and prerequisites.

Callback lifetime ↓Suspending a coroutine ↓Results and cancellation ↓

Callback lifetime

A registered callback may be called after the function that created it has returned. Its captures must therefore remain valid for the entire registration lifetime.

Capturing a local variable by reference is correct only if that variable lives long enough. The application owns registered callbacks; the objects they access need compatible lifetimes.

Suspending a coroutine

A coroutine can suspend execution with co_await while waiting for an operation to finish. Suspension neither creates a thread nor automatically moves expensive computation away from the current thread.

WebFront application tasks return webfront::Task. Start them with app.spawn(task) or ui.spawn(task). WebFront owns them and drains them before destruction.

Results and cancellation

The following fragment assumes a valid ui value and a JavaScript function registered as getTitle. The typed sender propagates the coroutine’s stop token. Retain the task’s TaskHandle to request individual cancellation.

Cancellation ends the local wait; it does not stop JavaScript that has already started. C++ futures and JavaScript promises do not expose this cancellation. Ordinary calls have no automatic timeout.

C++23
// Inside a webfront::Task coroutine:
auto title = co_await ui.jsFunctionSender<std::string>("getTitle")();
